newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Signs of Swiss recovery still lacking - SNB'S Rich.
newsitem.headline: Signs of Swiss recovery still lacking - SNB'S Rich.

text.p: Swiss National Bank (SNB) chief economist Georg Rich said the central bank still had no firm evidence that the Swiss economy was recovering even though it may have hit bottom late last year.

"Economic activity may have reached its cyclical trough in the third or fourth quarter of 1996, but we still lack firm evidence of a change for the better," he said in the text of a speech to be delivered at the City University of New York.
A copy of the text was distributed in Zurich.
SNB officials have said repeatedly the central bank would maintain its generous monetary policy until it had clear signs that the recession-bound economy was improving.
Rich said the Swiss franc exchange rate, after falling sharply in 1996, had stabilised at a level that should no longer inhibit the recovery of the Swiss economy.
"For this year, we expect the economy to return to a modest growth path," Rich said. He did not elaborate, but the SNB has forecast GDP will grow around 0.5 percent in 1997.
Rich said the economy, which has been more or less stagnant since 1991, was gathering strength to meet the challenges of globalisation.

"The rapidity and thoroughness of the (private sector's) structural change are largely responsible for the present poor performance of the Swiss economy," he said. "For this reason I do not regard the current stagnation as a sign of weakness.
"On the contrary, the Swiss economy is passing through a painful period of recuperation in order to regain the strength required to meet the challenges of the future."

He questioned whether the European Union should serve as a model for the relatively unregulated, free-market Swiss economy and expressed scepticism that the EU could solve the problem of sluggish economic growth by adopting a single currency.

"I sometimes wonder whether the EU is betting on the wrong horse by pushing monetary unification," he said. "In my view, the European economies would benefit more from reforms aimed directly at the cure of Eurosclerosis."
He singled out the need for radical reform of European laws to make the labour market more flexible, but noted the political will to adopt such unpopular measures seemed weak.

Rich reiterated the SNB's stance that it could relax monetary policy in the event of the planned launch of the single currency in 1999 sparking a strong speculative Swiss franc rise, as it had in 1995.
In the worst case, the SNB could temporarily peg the Swiss franc to the single "euro" currency.

"However, by placing a temporary ceiling on the Swiss franc exchange rate, the Swiss National Bank would lose control over the money supply and thus run the risk of triggering a subsequent rise in inflation," he said.
"We would regard a temporary peg only as a measure of last resort in the event of extreme exchange rate disturbances."
